reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: The most common urea cycle disorder and the only one that is X-linked, so severe disease predominantly affects hemizygous males
Affected male neonates classically appear well then develop lethargy, poor feeding, vomiting and encephalopathy with severe hyperammonaemia in the first days of life

Heterozygous females have a variable phenotype depending on X-inactivation and may present later with episodic hyperammonaemic crises, protein intolerance, migraine-like symptoms or psychiatric disturbance
The biochemical signature is hyperammonaemia with low or normal citrulline, elevated urine orotic acid, and typically a respiratory alkalosis without metabolic acidosis
Elevated orotic acid distinguishes OTC deficiency from carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 and N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiencies, in which orotic acid is not raised
Acute crises can be precipitated by infection, fasting, high protein load, surgery, or the postpartum period

Acute management follows urea cycle disorder principles: halt protein, reverse catabolism with glucose and lipid, give nitrogen scavengers and arginine, and use haemodialysis for severe hyperammonaemia
Because inheritance is X-linked rather than reflected by a single metabolite, standard newborn screening may miss cases, so a high index of suspicion and family testing are important
reference.pathophysiology: Ornithine transcarbamylase is a mitochondrial enzyme that combines carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to form citrulline, the second step of the urea cycle. Its deficiency, caused by mutations in the X-linked OTC gene, blocks ureagenesis and causes waste nitrogen to accumulate as ammonia. Because the block is proximal, carbamoyl phosphate builds up and is diverted into the pyrimidine synthesis pathway, generating excess orotic acid excreted in urine. Ammonia is neurotoxic, producing glutamine accumulation, astrocyte swelling and cerebral oedema. Females show a spectrum of severity determined by the pattern of X-chromosome inactivation in hepatocytes.
additionalDifferentials: Other urea cycle disorders (CPS1, NAGS, citrullinemia, argininosuccinic aciduria)
Reye-like syndrome and other causes of acute encephalopathy
Postpartum or valproate-associated hyperammonaemic encephalopathy in carrier females
additionalInvestigations: Urgent plasma ammonia and arterial blood gas (respiratory alkalosis)
Plasma amino acids (low citrulline, low arginine) and urine orotic acid (elevated)
Allopurinol loading or protein challenge to unmask carriers, used cautiously in specialist settings
Molecular testing of the OTC gene and enzyme assay on liver tissue where needed
Family screening and genetic counselling given X-linked inheritance
Neuroimaging in severe or prolonged hyperammonaemia
redFlags: Severe hyperammonaemic encephalopathy is a metabolic emergency mandating immediate ammonia lowering and often dialysis
Deteriorating consciousness, seizures or signs of cerebral oedema and raised intracranial pressure
A previously well neonatal boy collapsing after the first feeds, easily mistaken for sepsis
Carrier female with unexplained encephalopathy postpartum, after surgery, or on valproate
reference.prognosis: Neonatal-onset disease in boys is severe and, without rapid control of hyperammonaemia, carries a high risk of death or lasting neurodevelopmental impairment; later-onset and carrier presentations vary widely, and outcome depends on prompt recognition and management of crises, with liver transplantation offering definitive correction in selected patients.
pitfalls: Assuming females who are carriers are unaffected and overlooking symptomatic heterozygotes
Missing the diagnosis because newborn screening is insensitive for OTC deficiency
Delaying ammonia measurement in an encephalopathic patient and attributing illness to sepsis
Giving valproate or a high protein load to an undiagnosed carrier and precipitating a crisis
management: In an acute hyperammonaemic crisis, stop protein intake, give high-calorie glucose and lipid to suppress catabolism, and start intravenous nitrogen-scavenging agents (sodium benzoate and sodium phenylacetate) with intravenous arginine
Use haemodialysis or haemofiltration to clear ammonia rapidly in severe hyperammonaemia
Provide chronic management with a protein-restricted diet supplemented with essential amino acids, plus citrulline or arginine to support the urea cycle
Give long-term oral nitrogen scavengers (sodium phenylbutyrate or glycerol phenylbutyrate) to provide alternative routes for nitrogen excretion
Avoid known precipitants such as fasting, catabolic stress, high protein loads and sodium valproate, and supply a written emergency sick-day regimen
Offer liver transplantation as definitive treatment for severe or poorly controlled disease
Monitor plasma ammonia, amino acids and neurodevelopment within a metabolic multidisciplinary team, with genetic counselling and family screening given X-linked inheritance
